general.fact: The calfskin (parchment) was made between 1404 and 1438. This was found by radiocarbon dating of four small samples at the University of Arizona in 2009.
The radiocarbon date tells when the calf lived, not when the book was written or drawn. Greg Hodgins, who led the test, said nobody can tell how much time passed before the skin was used.
Many think the calfskin was used fairly soon, because good parchment was too valuable to leave unused for long. This is reasoning, not proof.

In 2009 McCrone Associates tested the ink and paints for Yale. The ink is iron gall ink. The blue paint is azurite, a ground-up blue mineral. The green is a copper-based colour. The paints were mixed with gum.
Nobody knows who drew the pictures. Most people who study the book think the drawings were made first and the text was written around them, but not everyone agrees.
Some think the paint was added later, perhaps much later, by a less careful "heavy painter" (an idea of Jorge Stolfi, reported by Nick Pelling). This is not settled.
Lisa Fagin Davis, a manuscript expert, has said she sees no sign that the paint itself is later.
The handwriting is thought to be by five scribes (Lisa Fagin Davis, 2020). The scribes may or may not be the same people as the artist or artists.
Nobody knows where the book was made. Some features have been linked to northern Italy, others to German-speaking lands; none of these links is proven.
The clothes and hairstyles of figures in other parts of the book have been compared with fashions of the early 1400s, which fits the radiocarbon date.
The bottom of the first page has a faded signature of Jacobus Horcicky de Tepenec, a chemist at the court of Emperor Rudolf II. It can be read under ultraviolet light.
